report:
Conclusion: Yes—when a large share of the population wears masks consistently, especially well-fitting surgical masks/respirators, the weight of evidence indicates reduced SARS-CoV-2 transmission, though the population-level effect is likely modest and depends heavily on compliance, mask quality, indoor exposure, and timing.

A PNAS evidence review concluded that “the preponderance of evidence” shows masks reduce transmissibility per contact and work best when compliance is high: https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2014564118. The strongest community randomized evidence is the Bangladesh cluster trial of ~342,000 adults: promoting masks tripled use and reduced symptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection, with larger benefits for surgical masks than cloth and among older adults: https://escholarship.org/uc/item/86t771h3.

However, certainty is not absolute. Cochrane’s review of randomized trials said it was “uncertain” whether masks slow respiratory-virus spread based on the limited trials assessed: https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD006207_do-physical-measures-such-hand-washing-or-wearing-masks-stop-or-slow-down-spread-respiratory-viruses. Cochrane later warned this was widely misinterpreted and should not be read as proof masks do not work: https://www.cochrane.org/about-us/news/statement-physical-interventions-interrupt-or-reduce-spread-respiratory-viruses-review.

Bottom line: masks are not a standalone fix, but broad, high-quality mask use during surges can reduce infections at the population level, particularly alongside ventilation, testing, and vaccination.
